Continuing: …"vahnayaḥ": here the affix "ni" comes by the Uṇādi-sūtra "vahi-śri-…" (as at p. 58); "n"-marked, so first-syllable acute. ॥९॥

Sūkta 3, The Tenth Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

पावका नः सरस्वती वाजेभिर्वाजिनीवती । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुः ॥१०॥

pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī vājebhir vājinīvatī | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ ||10||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

पावका । नः । सरस्वती । वाजेभिः । वाजिनीवती । यज्ञम् । वष्टु । धियावसुः ॥१०॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

सारस्वते तृचे या प्रथमा सान्वारम्भणीयेष्ट्या सरस्वत्याः पुरोनुवाक्या । तथा दर्शपूर्णमासारप्स्यमान इत्यस्मिन्कण्डे पावका नः सरस्वती पावीरवी कन्या चित्रायुः । आ. २-८ [?] । इति सूत्रितम् ॥ sārasvate tṛce yā prathamā sānvārambhaṇīyeṣṭyā sarasvatyāḥ puronuvākyā | tathā darśa-pūrṇamāsārapsyamāna ity asmin kaṇḍe pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ | ā. 2-8 [?] | iti sūtritam ||

Translation: "In the Sārasvata tṛca (the triplet addressed to Sarasvatī), the first Ṛk is the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā) of Sarasvatī in the "sānvārambhaṇīya" sacrificial offering; and likewise, in the section beginning "darśa-pūrṇamāsārapsyamāna" (one about to begin the new- and full-moon sacrifices), the Ṛks "pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī" and "pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ" are laid down in the sūtra (the source reference as printed is "ā. 2-8" [?])."

सरस्वती देवी वाजेभिर्हविर्लक्षणैरन्नैर्निमित्तभूतैः । यद्वा । यजमानेभ्यो दातव्यैरन्नैर्निमित्तभूतैः । नोऽस्मदीयं यज्ञं वष्टु । कामयताम् । कामयित्वा च निर्वहत्वित्यर्थः । तथा चारण्यककाण्डे श्रुत्यैव व्याख्यातम् । यज्ञं वष्टिवति यदाह यज्ञं वहत्विति तदाह । ऐ. आ. १-१-४ । इति । कीदृशी सरस्वती । पावका शोधयित्री वाजिनीवत्यन्नवत्क्रियावती धियावसुः कर्मप्राप्त्यधननिमित्तभूता । वाग्देवतायास्तथाविधं धननिमित्तत्वमारण्यककाण्डे श्रुत्या व्याख्यातम् । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुरिति वाग्वै धियावसुः । ऐ. आ. १-१-४ । इति । श्येनः सोमु [?] इत्यादिषु पञ्चत्रिंशत्संख्याकेषु देवताविशेषवाचिषु पदेषु सरमा सरस्वतीति पठितम् । एतामृचं यास्क एवं व्याचष्टे । पावका नः सरस्वत्यन्नैरन्नवती यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुः कर्मवसुः । नि. ११- … sarasvatī devī vājebhir havir-lakṣaṇair annair nimitta-bhūtaiḥ | yad vā | yajamānebhyo dātavyair annair nimitta-bhūtaiḥ | no 'smadīyaṃ yajñaṃ vaṣṭu | kāmayatām | kāmayitvā ca nirvahatv ity arthaḥ | tathā cāraṇyaka-kāṇḍe śrutyaiva vyākhyātam | yajñaṃ vaṣṭīvati yad āha yajñaṃ vahatv iti tad āha | ai. ā. 1-1-4 | iti | kīdṛśī sarasvatī | pāvakā śodhayitrī vājinīvaty annavat-kriyāvatī dhiyāvasuḥ karma-prāpty-adhana-nimitta-bhūtā | vāg-devatāyās tathāvidhaṃ dhana-nimittatvam āraṇyaka-kāṇḍe śrutyā vyākhyātam | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasur iti vāg vai dhiyāvasuḥ | ai. ā. 1-1-4 | iti | śyenaḥ somu [?] ity ādiṣu pañcatriṃśat-saṃkhyākeṣu devatā-viśeṣa-vāciṣu padeṣu saramā sarasvatīti paṭhitam | etām ṛcaṃ yāska evaṃ vyācaṣṭe | pāvakā naḥ sarasvaty annair annavatī yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ karma-vasuḥ | ni. 11- …

Translation: "'Sarasvatī' — the goddess — 'vājebhiḥ': by the oblation-nature foods that are the occasion (nimitta-bhūta) — or, by the foods to be given to the sacrificers, which are the occasion — 'may she desire our sacrifice ('vaṣṭu': let her desire it); and having desired it, let her carry it through' — such is the sense. And so the Āraṇyaka section itself explains this by Śruti: 'When it says "may she desire the sacrifice" ("yajñaṃ vaṣṭu"), it says "let her carry the sacrifice."' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 1-1-4). What kind of Sarasvatī? 'Pāvakā' — the purifier; 'vājinīvatī' — one possessing food, possessing activity; 'dhiyāvasuḥ' — one who is the occasion for the attaining of wealth through ritual action. That the goddess of speech is, in this way, the occasion of wealth, is explained by the Śruti in the Āraṇyaka section: '"yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ" — Speech indeed is "dhiyāvasuḥ."' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 1-1-4). Among the thirty-five words denoting particular deities, beginning with 'śyenaḥ somu [?],' 'saramā' and 'sarasvatī' are read. Yāska explains this Ṛk thus: '"Pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī": Sarasvatī, rich in foods; "yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ": let her desire the sacrifice, she whose wealth is ritual action.' (Nirukta 11-…)" Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Sanskrit printed in Kannada script; [?] where unclear. The sense lines are in three layers; the grammar is characterized with its sūtras kept.

original p. 65

Rik 3.10: close of the Bhāṣya (Nirukta quotation), grammar, Pada-meanings, Bhāvārtha, English rendering

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥ concluding the Nirukta quotation begun on p. 64

…३६ । इति ॥ …36 | iti ||

Translation: "(Nirukta 11-)36. — So much (of Yāska)." The number "36" is the continuation of the reference left open at the foot of p. 64.

Grammar of Rik 3.10 (characterized, with sūtras): - "Pāvakā": "pavanaṃ pāvaḥ śuddhiḥ; pāvaṃ kāyatīti pāvakā" — one who "sings/makes" purity ("kai gai rai śabde"); by आतोऽनुपसर्गे कः (āto 'nupasarge kaḥ, पा. ३-२-३) the affix "ka"; the accent of a kṛt-ending as second member gives an end-acute. Alternatively, in the sense "she purifies," with "ṇvul," the vowel "a" before the affix's "k" would normally become "i" (इदाप्यसुपः, id āpy asupaḥ, पा. ७-३-४४ [as printed "7-3-44"]), but that does not occur here, and the "aṃśa-udātta" accent is to be regarded as Vedic. - "Sarasvatī": "saras" from "sṛ" with the "asun" affix, hence first-syllable acute; "matup" and "ṅīp," being "p"-marked, are unaccented. - "Vājebhiḥ": "vāja" is first-syllable acute as belonging to the "vṛṣādi" class (an "ākṛti-gaṇa," an open-ended list). - "Vājinīvatī": "vājo 'nnam asty āsām" — "those [ritual] actions which possess food" = "vājinyaḥ kriyāḥ" [reading of the print: "vājo 'nnam āstīti vājinyaḥ kriyāḥ" ?]; by अत इनिठनौ (ata iniṭhanau, पा. ५-२-११५) the affix "ini"; "she who has those actions" = "vājinīvatī"; by छन्दसीरः (chandasīraḥ) "matup" gets "va"; since "matup" and "ṅīp" are "p"-marked and unaccented, only the "ini" affix's first-syllable acute remains. - "Yajñam": by यजयाचयतविच्छप्रच्छरक्षो नङ् (yaja-yāca-yata-vicchaprachcha-rakṣo naṅ, पा. ३-३-९०) the affix "naṅ"; end-acute by the affix. - "Vaṣṭu": root "vaś kāntau" (to desire; "kānti" = wish); by आदिप्रभृतिभ्यः शपः (ādi-prabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ) "śap" is elided (luk); nighāta. - "Dhiyāvasuḥ": "dhiyā karmaṇā vasu yasyāḥ sakāśād bhavati sā dhiyāvasuḥ" — she from whom wealth comes by ritual action; the case-ending is acute by सावेकाचः (sāv ekācaḥ); in a bahuvrīhi, by बहुव्रीहौ प्रकृत्या पूर्वपदम् (bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam), the case-accent alone remains; the retention of the instrumental ending (a-luk) is Vedic.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

पावका (pāvakā) — one who purifies (people), or who cleanses | वाजिनीवती (vājinīvatī) — (to the people who praise) one who has food and sustenance and gives them | धियावसुः (dhiyāvasuḥ) — she who is the cause of wealth and the like, the fruit of sacrifice and the other rites | सरस्वती (sarasvatī) — the goddess Sarasvatī (the goddess of speech, or the river named Sarasvatī) | नः (naḥ) — our | यज्ञम् (yajñam) — the sacrifice | वाजेभिः (vājebhiḥ) — through the foods that take the form of the oblation | वष्टु (vaṣṭu) — let her desire (let her bring the sacrifice to completion, with all its parts).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

The goddess Sarasvatī is the purifier of people; she gives food and the like to the people who worship her by sacrifice and the like; and she is the cause of the attainment of lordship in the form of wealth. May such a Sarasvatī, satisfied with the foods and the like, in the form of the oblation that we give, bring our sacrifice to its full completion.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"May Saraswati, the purifier, the bestower of food, recompenser of worships with wealth, be attracted to our rite by our offer of sacrificial food." original p. 66

Special topics on Rik 3.10: the Sārasvata tṛca; the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

This Ṛk, "pāvakā naḥ," together with the following two Ṛks, form the "sārasvata-tṛcaḥ," that is, three Ṛks that relate to Sarasvatī. Of these three Ṛks, the first, "pāvakā naḥ," is the "puronuvākyā" mantra for invoking Sarasvatī in the special sacrificial offering called the Anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi. In a sacrifice, when oblation is made to any god, two Ṛks are used; both must relate to that deity. With the first Ṛk — recited aloud — the deity is invoked; this Ṛk is called "puronuvākyā." With another Ṛk the oblation is made to that deity; this mantra is called "yājyā." Likewise, in the Anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi both Ṛks, "puronuvākyā" and "yājyā," are used. This matter the great sage Āśvalāyana has stated thus in his Śrauta-sūtra (Āśv. Śrau. Sū. 2-8), in the section beginning "darśapūrṇamāsārapsyamāna":

पावका नः सरस्वती पावीरवी कन्या चित्रायुः । (आश्व. २-८) pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ | (āśv. 2-8) Gloss: "'Pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī' and 'pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ'." (The sūtra simply names the two Ṛks to be used.)

Before performing this Anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, the sacrificer must first perform the rites called puṇyāhavācana, nāndīśrāddha and udakaśānti, tie a thread called pratisara on his wife's hand, and then, on the day following, after performing the daily rites such as bathing, he must make the resolution: "yāvajjīvaṃ darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yakṣye" (यावज्जीवं दर्शपूर्णमासाभ्यां यक्ष्ये — yāvaj-jīvaṃ darśa-pūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yakṣye — "as long as I live I shall sacrifice with the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices"). Next he makes the resolution "anvārambhaṇīyayā yakṣye" (अन्वारम्भणीयया यक्ष्ये — "I shall sacrifice with the anvārambhaṇīyā") and must perform the rite called agnyanayana — bringing in the fire from the Gārhapatya fire by the "agni-viharaṇa." Then, in speaking of the "anvādhāna," the chief ("pradhāna") oblation is made to the principal deities Agnāviṣṇū, Sarasvatī, Sarasvān, and Agnir-bhagī [?] (the last name as printed; I am not sure of it). The offering-materials are: for Agnāviṣṇū, "ekādaśa-kapāla puroḍāśa" (a cake on eleven potsherds); for the deity Sarasvatī, a "caru" (cooked rice-offering); for Sarasvān, a "dvādaśa-kapāla puroḍāśa" (twelve potsherds); and for the deity "Agnir-bhagī [?]," an "aṣṭādaśa-kapāla puroḍāśa" (eighteen potsherds). The "puronuvākyā" and "yājyā" mantras used when making oblation to these deities are these: The page continues on p. 67 with the remaining oblations. अग्नाविष्णू — अग्नाविष्णू सजोषसा (पुरोनुवाक्या) · अग्नाविष्णू महि धाम (याज्या) agnāviṣṇū — agnāviṣṇū sajoṣasā (puronuvākyā) · agnāviṣṇū mahi dhāma (yājyā) सरस्वती — पावकानः सरस्वती (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. १-३-१० · पावीरवीकन्या (याज्या) ऋ. सं. ६-४९-७ [?] sarasvatī — pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 1-3-10 · pāvīravī kanyā (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 6-49-7 [?] सरस्वान् — पीपिवांसं सरस्वतः (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. ७-९६-६ [?] · दिव्यं सुपर्णं वायसम् (याज्या) ऋ. सं. १-१६४-५२ [?] sarasvān — pīpivāṃsaṃ sarasvataḥ (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 7-96-6 [?] · divyaṃ suparṇaṃ vāyasam (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 1-164-52 [?] Gloss (mine): "Agnā-Viṣṇū: 'Agni and Viṣṇu, of one mind…' / 'Agni and Viṣṇu, the great abode…'; Sarasvatī: 'Our purifier Sarasvatī…' / 'The purifier, the maiden…'; Sarasvān: 'Sarasvān who is full of [waters]…' / 'The divine, fair-winged bird…'." The Anvārambhaṇīyā mantras (concluded); "pāvakā" and its use for different deities

अग्निर्भगी [?] — आसवं सवितुः (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. ७-१०३-६ [?] · स नो राधांस्या भर (याज्या) ऋ. सं. २-३५-११ [?] agnir-bhagī [?] — āsavaṃ savituḥ (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 7-103-6 [?] · sa no rādhāṃsyā bhara (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 2-35-11 [?] Gloss: "(Of Savitṛ) the impulsion of Savitṛ…" / "Bring us, then, bounties…" [tentative; only opening words are given]

That is: in this Anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi, when the goddess Sarasvatī is invoked, the Ṛk

पावकानः सरस्वती वाजेभिर्वाजिनीवती । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-३-१०) pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī vājebhir vājinīvatī | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-3-10) (= the present Rik 3.10; translated above.)

is to be used as the puronuvākyā mantra, and the Ṛk

पावीरवी कन्या चित्रायुः सरस्वती वीरपत्नी धियं धात् । ग्नाभिरच्छिद्रं शरणं सजोषा दुराधर्षं गृणते शर्म यंसत् ॥ (ऋ. सं. ६-४९-७) pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ sarasvatī vīrapatnī dhiyaṃ dhāt | gnābhir acchidraṃ śaraṇaṃ sajoṣā durādharṣaṃ gṛṇate śarma yaṃsat || (ṛ. saṃ. 6-49-7) Gloss (mine): "May Sarasvatī, the maiden, of wondrous life, the hero's consort, grant insight; may she, in concert with the goddess-wives, grant to the singer a shelter without a gap, hard to assail." [tentative]

is to be used as the yājyā mantra — so it is said.

पावका (pāvakā) — This word is derived from the root "pūñ" ("to purify, to cleanse"). The Bhāṣyakāra gives its derivation as "pavanaṃ pāvaḥ śuddhiḥ, taṃ kāyatīti pāvakā" (पवनं पावः शुद्धिस्तं कायतीति पावका — "'pāva' is purification; she who 'makes' that is 'pāvakā'"), i.e., one who purifies; one who cleanses, removing sins. Though the word "pāvaka" is used in many places of deities such as Agni, the Maruts and Soma, it is used especially of Agni: Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers: every number in the five lists below is marked as best-effort; the print is in small Kannada numerals and many digits are uncertain. English words are as printed in the source.

Agni — अग्ने पावक रोचिषा मन्द्रया देव जिह्वया । (ऋ. सं. ५-२६-१) agne pāvaka rociṣā mandrayā deva jihvayā | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-26-1) Gloss: "O purifying Agni, with your light, with your joyful tongue, O god."

स नः पावक दीदिवोऽग्ने देवाँ इहावह । (ऋ. सं. १-१२-१०) sa naḥ pāvaka dīdivo 'gne devāṁ ihāvaha | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-12-10) Gloss: "O shining purifier, bring the gods here."

अस्या जरासो दमा मरित्रा अर्चद्धूमासो अग्नयः पावकाः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-९१-२ [?]) asyā jarāso damā maritrā arcaddhūmāso agnayaḥ pāvakāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 10-91-2 [?]) Gloss: "…the purifying fires, with smoke…" [tentative; the first half is not clear to me]

Indra — मिहः पावकाः प्रतता अभूवन्त्स्वस्ति नः पिपृहि पारमासाम् । (ऋ. सं. ३-३१-१० [?]) mihaḥ pāvakāḥ pratatā abhūvan svasti naḥ pipṛhi pāram āsām | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-31-10 [?]) Gloss: "The purifying showers have spread out; carry us safely across them."

Uṣas — व्यू व्रजस्य तमसो द्वारोच्छन्तीरव्रञ्छुचयः पावकाः ॥ (ऋ. सं. ४-५१-२ [?]) vy ū vrajasya tamaso dvāroc chantīr avran śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 4-51-2 [?]) Gloss: "Shining, they have opened the doors of the dark pen — the bright, purifying (dawns)." [tentative]

Āpaḥ (the Waters) — समुद्रार्था याः शुचयः पावकास्ता आपो देवीरिह मामवन्तु ॥ (ऋ. सं. ७-४९-३) samudrārthā yāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakās tā āpo devīr iha mām avantu || (ṛ. saṃ. 7-49-3) Gloss: "Those pure, purifying waters that go to the sea — may those divine waters protect me here."

original p. 68

"pāvakā" (concluded); "sarasvatī" — the five senses of the word (opening)

In these and other mantras, the word "pāvaka" is used of different deities. Western scholars have explained this word with such words as : "Purifier, purifying, bright, glittering, pure, sacred, blazing, flaming." In the sense relating to Agni, both senses — "that which purifies" and "that which shines" — may be said.

सरस्वती (sarasvatī) — Sāyaṇācārya has given a five-fold account of the sense of the word "sarasvatī" as used in the Ṛgveda mantras:

  1. Nadī (a river) — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-142 [?]-9 [?]; 1-164 [?]-52 [?]; 2-30-8 [?].
  2. The name of a river — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-3-12 [?]; 2-41-16 [?]; 3-23-4 [?]; 6-61 [?] (the 4th, 7th, 10th, 11th and 13th Ṛks of it [?]); 6-52-6 [?]; 6-61-2 [?]; 7-36-6 [?]; 7-95-1 and 2 [?]; 7-96-1 [?]; 8-21-17 and 18 [?]; 10-64-9 [?]; 10-65-13 [?].
  3. The name of a deity — Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-43-11 [?]; 5-46-2 [?]; 6-49-7 [?]; 5-30-12 [?]; 10-17-7 [?]; 10-90-12 [?].
  4. An ākāśābhimāni-devatā (a deity presiding over the sky-region) — "(one of the three goddesses Iḷā, Bhāratī and Sarasvatī)" — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-188-8 [?].
  5. Vāgdevī (the goddess of Speech) — Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-11 [?]; 3-4-8 [?]; 3-54-13 [?]; 5-42-12 [?]; 7-39-5 [?]; 7-40-3 [?] and others [?].

In the Ṛgveda there are many mantras praising the goddess Sarasvatī. But on the question "who is this goddess Sarasvatī, and what is her nature?" the author of the Nirukta (Yāska) has said nothing; he has said only: "nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti" (नदीवद्देवतावच्च निगमा भवन्ति — nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti — "there are Vedic passages (that treat her) as a river and as a deity"). That is: in some mantras that have the deity Sarasvatī as their subject she is described as a river, and in some as a deity. But it is not clear whether the river named Sarasvatī is regarded as a goddess and praised, or the goddess is regarded as a river and praised. Therefore it must be said that "Sarasvatī" points to both river and deity. In the view that Sarasvatī is a deity, the questions — who is that deity? what is her nature? what are her station and abodes? — cannot easily be answered with a fitting reply. In the view that Sarasvatī is a river, it may be said that a river of that famous name existed in ancient times (the source adds in English: "the modern Sarsuti") and that this very river is praised in the Ṛgveda. When it is said so, a doubt arises: in the sacrifices and the like performed for the sake of particular deities, would not the praise of inanimate things such as rivers be forbidden? … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers in small Kannada numerals marked [?] where uncertain.

original p. 69

Sarasvatī as river and as deity: the Mīmāṃsā question; five views of the goddess

Continuing from p. 68, at the doubt whether praise of inanimate things like rivers would be forbidden in sacrifices: …"That doubt can be answered. On this point the sage Jaimini, in his Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, raised the objection ("pūrvapakṣa") on the basis of "acetane 'rtha-bandhanāt" (अचेतनेऽर्थबन्धनात् — acetane 'rtha-bandhanāt, जै. सू. १-२-३५ [?]) — that is, that where mantras address inanimate things, the connection of sense is [impossible]. To this the Bhāṣyakāra (the Vedāntic commentator) has given the answer by citing the Vedānta-sūtra "abhimāni-vyapadeśaḥ" (अभिमानिव्यपदेशः — abhimāni-vyapadeśaḥ, वे. सू. २-१-५): that is, wherever, in Veda-mantras, inanimate things are addressed, it is to be understood that what is said is addressed to the presiding deities ("abhimāni-devatā") of those inanimate things. (See Part 1, pp. 380–381.) Hence, where a river is praised, it is to be understood that its presiding deity is praised. Concerning this goddess Sarasvatī many persons hold many different views:

  1. In the Purāṇas and elsewhere, "Sarasvatī" means "vāg-adhiṣṭhātrī, śāradā, vidyā-svarūpiṇī, haṃsa-vāhinī" (वागधिष्ठात्री शारदा विद्यास्वरूपिणी हंसवाहिनी) — a particular deity: the presiding deity of speech, famous by the name Śāradā, embodying learning, seated on a swan.
  2. Or: this goddess Sarasvatī is the Āditya (the Sun) specially qualified by a limiting condition ("upādhi"); "upādhi" here means the twilight. So some hold that the Sun, shining at twilight, is here praised in the form of Sarasvatī.
  3. The word "saras" comes from the root "sṛ" (to move, to flow): "saro 'syā asti" or "sarastejo yasyā vidyate sā sarasvatī" — she who has "saras" (radiance, fluid motion) — she who shines in the form of radiance is therefore called "Sarasvatī."
  4. Or (the source quotes Sanskrit here):

अथवा — प्रातर्वाचां प्रवर्तिका, प्राणिनां स्वापपरित्यागेन स्फोचित [?] व्यवहारेषु प्रवृत्तौ तब्दायमानतायोः [?] प्रवृत्तेः, रात्रौ च वाचां निरोधिका रात्रौ प्राणिनां निलायनिलीनत्वेन सुस्वतया [?] शब्दविरामात् । एवं च शब्दस्य प्रवर्तिका निवर्तिका एषैव लोके सरस्वतीत्वेन व्यपदिश्यते नान्या ॥ athavā — prātar vācāṃ pravartikā, prāṇināṃ svāpa-parityāgena sphocita [?] vyavahāreṣu pravṛttau tabdāyamānatāyoḥ [?] pravṛtteḥ, rātrau ca vācāṃ nirodhikā rātrau prāṇināṃ nilāya-nilīnatvena susvatayā [?] śabda-virāmāt | evaṃ ca śabdasya pravartikā nivartikā eṣaiva loke sarasvatītvena vyapadiśyate nānyā ||

(Reading note: the middle of this Sanskrit sentence is garbled in the print, and the words I mark [?] are my best letter-by-letter reading, not a restoration; the opening "prātar vācāṃ pravartikā" and the close "evaṃ ca śabdasya pravartikā nivartikā eṣaiva loke sarasvatītvena vyapadiśyate nānyā" are clear.)

Translation of the clear parts, with the Kannada gloss that follows it: "Or: she is the prompter of speech in the morning … and at night the restrainer of speech … and thus, as both the prompter and the stopper of sound, she alone is in the world called Sarasvatī and no other." The Kannada explains: "In the morning the creatures, rising from sleep, set about talking and about their several affairs and activities; at night, the creatures are overcome by sleep, and so, apart from talking and making sounds, they come to rest from their activities and dealings. Therefore, because she is the cause of beginning and ending in the matter of talking or making sound, this goddess of speech is called Sarasvatī."

(5) — continued on p. 70. Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure. English words as printed.

original p. 70

Sarasvatī: the fifth view (Uṣas); the three questions to be considered; Sarasvatī in Rik 3.10–12; the ṛṣis

  1. As stated before, since the powers of speech and the like belong to this deity, this goddess Sarasvatī is in the form of Uṣas (Dawn). For this very reason, among the words that are the names of the goddess Uṣas — sūnṛtā, sūnṛtāvatī, sūnṛtāvarī and others — the name of this goddess Sarasvatī occurs. Here the word "sūnṛta" means words that are both pleasant and true.

In just this way, in the question of the goddess Sarasvatī, Śaunaka, the author of the Bṛhaddevatā, and other authors have explained her in various ways.

Now let us examine briefly in what senses the word "sarasvatī" has been used in the Ṛgveda. In this matter three points must be attended to: (1) the Ṛk we are now expounding, "pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī"; (2) the other Ṛks having Sarasvatī as their deity; (3) the ṛṣis who composed these Ṛks, and their lineages. We shall weigh these three matters.

In the sūkta now in hand, the Ṛks 10, 11 and 12 are mantras addressed to Sarasvatī. In the Ṛks 10 and 11, Sarasvatī is probably regarded as a deity and praised; in the 12th Ṛk, as the river. The Bhāṣyakāra Sāyaṇācārya explains Sarasvatī in the Ṛks 10–11 as the goddess of speech, and in the 12th Ṛk as the presiding deity of the river called Sarasvatī. Griffith explains "Sarasvatī" as the goddess of speech; but where "pāvakā" is given the sense "purifying with water," and where "ārṇa" [the word in Rik 3.12, "maho arṇaḥ"] is given the sense "river," "Sarasvatī" must mean a river, or the presiding deity of a river. Some modern scholars hold that "Sarasvatī" means the river Sindhu. But since the hermitage of the sage Madhucchandas, son of Viśvāmitra, who composed this Ṛk, was on the western bank of the present river Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra — as stated in the Mahābhārata (Śalya-parva, adhyāya 3[?]) — it is possible to conjecture that Madhucchandas praised this very river Sarasvatī: for when a person praises a river, it does not seem reasonable that he should leave aside the well-known river near the place where he lives and praise some other river of the same name far away.

In the second Maṇḍala, the Ṛks that have Sarasvatī as their deity — Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-3[?]-8 [?]; 2-3[?]-8 [?]; and 2-41-16[?] to 18 [?] — were all composed by the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada, son of Śunahotra. This ṛṣi Gṛtsamada is understood to be the sixth in descent from the sage Atri (according to the book "Pravara and Gotra," No. 25 of the Mysore Government Oriental Library, as the source says); Viśvāmitra is the fifth in descent from Atri. In all, in eight Ṛks, this ṛṣi Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī… Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." All Ṛg-vedic reference-numbers on this page are best-effort readings of small Kannada numerals and are marked [?] collectively here and in the text; none should be relied on without checking the page. English words as printed.

original p. 71

The ṛṣis who praise Sarasvatī: Gṛtsamada (continued), Devaśravas and Devavāta, Bharadvāja

Continuing from p. 70: …Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-11 [?] and 2-3-8 [?] he praises Sarasvatī together with Iḷā and Bhāratī. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-3[?]-8 [?] he speaks of these three — that is, Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī — as three goddesses. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-3[?]-5 [?] he praises Sarasvatī along with Indra and the Maruts. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-3[?]-8 [?] he speaks of Sarasvatī as an exalted deity. In the 18th Ṛk [?] of the sūkta 2-4[?] he describes Sarasvatī as a very large river and also a very large deity; and in the 15th Ṛk [?] he describes her, with the word "ṛtāvarī" (that is, "ṛta" = water) as a river with abundant water. Seeing this, some Western scholars say, because she is spoken of as "a very large river," that she must be the Sindhu. But that is not right; for when a poet praises a river or a deity (even a small or ordinary one) it is common to describe it as very large. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-3[?]-8 [?] some think the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī as the presiding deity of both rivers and the (cloud) lightning; but to say that one ṛṣi describes one and the same deity in different senses seems without reason.

The sūkta Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-23 [?] has as ṛṣis Devaśravas and Devavāta, the sons of Bharata. According to the book "Gotra-Pravara" mentioned earlier, these ṛṣis are understood to be the sons of Viśvāmitra. Bharata is understood, from the same book, to be the sixth in descent from Atri, and Viśvāmitra the seventh [as the print says; compare the "fifth" for Viśvāmitra on p. 70 — the discrepancy is in the source and is recorded, not resolved]; both are descendants of Purūravas, son of Atri's [line] and the son of Budha (the source says: "of Atri's grandson [?], Purūravas") — the exact genealogical phrasing is unclear in the print. These ṛṣis in Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-23-4 [?] say:

नि त्वा दधे वर आ पृथिव्या इळायास्पदे सुदिनत्वे अह्नाम् । दृषद्वत्यां मानुषा आपयायां सरस्वत्यां रेवदग्ने दिदीहि ॥ (ऋ. सं. ३-२३-४) ni tvā dadhe vara ā pṛthivyā iḷāyās pade sudinatve ahnām | dṛṣadvatyāṃ mānuṣā āpayāyāṃ sarasvatyāṃ revad agne didīhi || (ṛ. saṃ. 3-23-4) Gloss (mine): "I have set you down on the best place of the earth, on the footing of Iḷā, in the good days of the days; on the Dṛṣadvatī, among men, on the Āpayā, on the Sarasvatī: shine richly, O Agni."

Along with the river Sarasvatī they name two other rivers: Dṛṣadvatī and Āpayā. Dṛṣadvatī is the present river called Citrāṅga (the source's English: "the modern Chitrang, Chautag, or Chitang"); Āpayā is the present river called Apagā ("the modern Apaga"). Since both rivers lie in the neighbourhood of the river Sarasvatī, it can be said with confidence that Sarasvatī is not the Sindhu. Further, the hermitage of the sage Viśvāmitra, too, was on the west bank of this river Sarasvatī (in Kurukṣetra), as modern investigations show (the source adds: "see Dey's Geographical Dic."). All that has been said so far concerns the lineages of Atri and Viśvāmitra.

Now let us consider Bharadvāja and his lineage. The three Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-49-7 [?]; 6-50-12 [?]; 6-52-6 [?] all have, as their ṛṣi, Ṛjiśvā, the son of Bharadvāja. In the first and third of these three Ṛks, Sarasvatī is [described as] a river… Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure.

original p. 72

Sarasvatī as a river in the hymns of Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha and Śobhari

…the matter is stated clearly. In the second mantra, though the name of Sarasvatī is mentioned along with the names of the deities Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vāyu and Parjanya, Sarasvatī may be understood as a river; for in the two [other] Ṛks the ṛṣi says that Sarasvatī is a river, and in another Ṛk the same ṛṣi praises Sarasvatī as a river — which is only natural. The hermitage of Bharadvāja was at Prayāga (the source's English: "Allahabad"). Therefore Ṛjiśvā, son of Bharadvāja, must have praised a river near his own hermitage. The whole of Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-61 [?] (14 [?] Ṛks in all) by the ṛṣi Bharadvāja concerns Sarasvatī. Some Western scholars hold that the sense of several words in this sūkta applies to the river Sindhu; but since those words apply equally to the river Sarasvatī, there is no room for doubt.

The Ṛks in the seventh Maṇḍala — Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-9[?]-5 [?]; 7-3[?]-11 [?]; 7-3[?]-6 [?]; 7-4[?]-3 [?]; 7-6[?]-5 [?] and others [?] — are all by the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha. The hermitage of Vasiṣṭha is understood to have been near Mount Abu (the source's English), a hill in the Āravalī mountain in Rājputānā. The first four mantras and the last two sūktas [of the group] praise Sarasvatī as a river. The words "sindhumātā" and "āsamudrāt" in these Ṛks apply especially to the river Sindhu, and so some say that it is the Sindhu that is praised in these mantras. This dispute cannot be completely set aside. Still, when speaking of one river, it is not impossible to compare another river with it, and to praise it with exaggeration.

In the eighth Maṇḍala, the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-2[?]-17 and 18 [?] are by the ṛṣi Śobhari, son of Kaṇva. In these Ṛks this ṛṣi describes the sacrifice that a king named Citra performed on the bank of the river Sarasvatī and praises that king's gifts. Since Śaunaka, in his Bṛhaddevatā (6-3[?] to 6-3[?]), says that this king Citra performed a sacrifice at Kurukṣetra, the river must be the nearby Sarasvatī. And:

पूषा विष्णुर्हवनं मे सरस्वत्यवन्तु सप्त सिन्धवः । आपो वातः पर्वतासो वनस्पतिः शृणोतु पृथिवी हवम् ॥ (ऋ. सं. ८-५४-४ [?]) pūṣā viṣṇur havanaṃ me sarasvaty avantu sapta sindhavaḥ | āpo vātaḥ parvatāso vanaspatiḥ śṛṇotu pṛthivī havam || (ṛ. saṃ. 8-54-4 [?]) Gloss (mine): "May Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, the seven rivers, help my invocation; the Waters, the Wind, the Mountains, the Tree-lord — may Earth hear my call."

In this Ṛk, Sarasvatī is also mentioned among the deities Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, the Seven Rivers (sapta-sindhavaḥ), the Waters, the Wind, the Mountains, the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati) and Earth. Likewise in Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-9[?]-3 [?], the ṛṣi of that mantra, Vasiṣṭha or Pavitra, has used the word "Sarasvatī." Here Sarasvatī may be taken in either sense, as a deity or as a river. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-30-12 [?], it is clearly stated which river is meant by "Sarasvatī" … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure. The modern river-names in brackets are printed in English in the source. The Sanskrit mnemonic verses on this page are compressed and partly garbled in the print: They are transcribed as read, with [?], and their sense is given in outline rather than as a line-by-line translation.

original p. 73

Sarasvatī among the rivers (Ṛ. 10-75); the ten Āprī-sūktas (opening of the list)

Continuing from p. 72, "…it is clearly stated which river is meant by 'Sarasvatī':" In Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-64-9 [?] the ṛṣi of that mantra, Gaya (of the lineage of Atri), speaks of Sarasvatī in the company of the rivers Sindhu and Sarayū (the source's English: "Gogra"). And:

इमं मे गङ्गे यमुने सरस्वति शुतुद्रि स्तोमं सचता परुष्ण्या । असिक्न्या मरुद्वृधे वितस्तयार्जीकीये शृणुह्या सुषोमया ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-७५-५) imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri stomaṃ sacatā paruṣṇyā | asiknyā marudvṛdhe vitastayārjīkīye śṛṇuhy ā suṣomayā || (ṛ. saṃ. 10-75-5) Gloss (mine): "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudri — attend to this my praise, together with Paruṣṇī; with Asiknī, O Marudvṛdhā, with Vitastā, O Ārjīkīyā, hear, together with Suṣomā."

In this Ṛk the river Sarasvatī is named together with Gaṅgā (the Ganges), Yamunā (the Jamna), Śutudri (the Sutlej), Paruṣṇī (the Ravi), Asiknī (the Chinab), Vitastā (the Jhelam), Marudvṛdhā (the United Stream of the Jhelam and Chenab), Ārjīkīyā (the Bias) and Suṣomā (the Indus) — all in the source's English — and from this it is plain that the river Sarasvatī is one distinct river of her own and is not the Sindhu. The entire sūkta in which the above Ṛk occurs is about rivers: all the Ṛks of this sūkta [the number is printed "9" — read with caution] have rivers for their deities. The ṛṣi of this sūkta is Sindhukṣit, the son of Priyamedha.

Sarasvatī is spoken of in the Āprī-sūktas as one of the three goddesses called "tisro devyaḥ." In the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā there are ten sūktas that are called Āprī-sūktas. In Śaunaka's Anuvākānukramaṇī the particulars of these sūktas are given thus:

श्लोकस्याश्य [?] यथासंख्यं सूक्तानि दश वै विदुः । न आ वहाग्न आ वहाद्य राजसेत्यग्निर्नि [?] च । समित्समित्सु शोचिषे जुषस्व विश्वतस्तथा । इमां मे अद्य [?] मन्विमा यूर्धर्षिपक्ष [?] आप्रियः ॥ वसिष्ठशुनकौ विना समिद्धः सर्वपक्षताः [?] । जुषस्वादित्तीययया [?] तनूनपाद्विरोधिता [?] । यजुः श्रुतौ तथाश्रुतेः समिद्धे सूक्तमध्यतः । प्रजापतेः पशोः सदा भवेयुरद्य मन्विमाः ॥ इतीरितं हि बह्वृचैर्यथर्षि वेति सूत्रतः ॥

ślokasyāśya [?] yathā-saṃkhyaṃ sūktāni daśa vai viduḥ | na ā vahāgna ā vahādya rājasety agnir ni [?] ca | samit-samit-su śociṣe juṣasva viśvatas tathā | imāṃ me adya [?] manvimā yūrdharṣi-pakṣa [?] āpriyaḥ || vasiṣṭha-śunakau vinā samiddhaḥ sarva-pakṣatāḥ [?] | juṣasvādittīyayayā [?] tanūnapād-virodhitā [?] | yajuḥ śrutau tathā-śruteḥ samiddhe sūkta-madhyataḥ | prajāpateḥ paśoḥ sadā bhaveyur adya manvimāḥ | itīritaṃ hi bahvṛcair yathā-ṛṣi veti sūtrataḥ ||

Outline of the sense (not a line-by-line translation — the verses are a compressed mnemonic, and several words are garbled in the print): the verses state that there are ten such sūktas, "in order of number," and give them by their opening words ("na ā vaha," "ā vaha," "rājasi," "agnir nihitaḥ," and so on); they note which of them are by Vasiṣṭha and Śunaka (Śaunaka); they note how the Yajus and Śruti texts treat "samiddha" in the middle of the sūkta; and they say that, as the Ṛgvedins' sūtra puts it, the sūktas are recited "according to the ṛṣi."

Of the sūktas listed above, the sūktas numbered 1–2 have 12 and 13 Ṛks; all the rest have 11 Ṛks. The deities of these 11 Ṛks are as follows:

Ṛk Deity (Sanskrit as printed) Meaning
1 इध्मः समिद्धोऽग्निर्वा (idhmaḥ samiddho 'gnir vā) Idhma, i.e., the kindled Agni
2 तनूनपात् (tanūnapāt) Tanūnapāt
3 इळः (iḷaḥ) Iḷa
4 बर्हिः (barhiḥ) the Barhis (sacred grass)
5 देवीर्द्वारः (devīr dvāraḥ) the divine Doors
6 उषासानक्ता (uṣāsānaktā) Dawn and Night
7 दैव्यौ होतारौ प्रचेतसौ (daivyau hotārau pracetasau) the two divine, wise Hotṛs
8 तिस्रो देव्यः सरस्वतीळाभारत्यः (tisro devyaḥ sarasvatī-iḷā-bhāratyaḥ) the three goddesses: Sarasvatī, Iḷā, Bhāratī
9 त्वष्टा (tvaṣṭā) Tvaṣṭṛ
10 वनस्पतिः (vanaspatiḥ) Vanaspati
11 स्वाहाकृतयः (svāhākṛtayaḥ) the Svāhā-offerings

In the first sūkta with 12 Ṛks, the deity Narāśaṃsa is also present; in the second sūkta, with 13 Ṛks, both Narāśaṃsa and Indra are deities; therefore, in place of the 11 Ṛks of the other sūktas, these have 12 and 13. In the other matters there is no difference — only the metres and the ṛṣis differ. In the animal sacrifice (paśuyāga), while praising Agni (the "samiddha-agni") and while performing the eleven prayāja homas, these sūktas are recited. In these sūktas, "tisro devyaḥ" means the praise of the three goddesses Iḷā, Sarasvatī, Bhāratī. The chief point to be noted here is that Agni is worshipped in three forms: on earth, in the atmosphere, and in heaven. Since Bhāratī indicates the rays of the Sun, this deity (that is, the Sun) is the form of Agni in heaven. Sarasvatī … for lightning, the one presiding … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers are in small Kannada numerals and are marked [?] where uncertain. original p. 75

"tisro devyaḥ"; Rigvedic verses that treat Sarasvatī as a deity rather than a river

Continuing from p. 74, "Sarasvatī … for lightning, the one presiding…" …Because Sarasvatī is described in many places as a presiding deity of the lightning (vidyud-abhimānī-devatā), this Sarasvatī is the form of Agni in the atmosphere. Because the goddess Iḷā gives to the people on earth wealth and the like and long life, this goddess is the form of Agni on earth: such is the signification of these three, Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī. The ṛṣis praise these three goddesses, asking them to come to the sacrificial altar and sit on the "barhis" (spread darbha-grass).

Here are some examples of verses in which the ṛṣis praise Sarasvatī as a deity other than a river: Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure. English words and the bibliographic list are as printed in the source.

  1. तान्पूर्वया निविदा हूमहे वयं भगं मित्रमदितिं दक्षमस्रिधम् । अर्यमणं वरुणं सोममश्विना सरस्वती नः सुभगा मयस्करत् ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-८९-३) tān pūrvayā nividā hūmahe vayaṃ bhagaṃ mitram aditiṃ dakṣam asridham | aryamaṇaṃ varuṇaṃ somam aśvinā sarasvatī naḥ subhagā mayas karat || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-89-3) Gloss: "Those (gods) we invoke with the ancient invocation — Bhaga, Mitra, Aditi, the undecaying Dakṣa, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Soma, the Aśvins; may fortunate Sarasvatī make us happy." (The source's remark:) In this Ṛk Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech, or the presiding deity of lightning.

  2. सरस्वति त्वमस्माँ अविड्ढि मरुत्वती धृषती जेषि शत्रून् । (ऋ. सं. २-३०-८) sarasvati tvam asmāṁ aviḍḍhi marutvatī dhṛṣatī jeṣi śatrūn | (ṛ. saṃ. 2-30-8) Gloss: "O Sarasvatī, protect us; accompanied by the Maruts, bold, you conquer the foes."

  3. सरस्वती शृणवन्यज्ञियासो धाता रयिं सहवीरं तुराषाट् । (ऋ. सं. ३-३४-१३ [?]) sarasvatī śṛṇavan yajñiyāso dhātā rayiṃ sahavīraṃ turāṣāṭ | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-34-13 [?]) Gloss: "May Sarasvatī hear — (the gods) worthy of sacrifice — bestowing wealth with heroes, the swift conqueror." [tentative; the print's wording of this line differs a little from what I would expect, and I give it as printed]

(The source's remark on (2) and (3):) In these Ṛks Sarasvatī is regarded either as a river or as the presiding deity of lightning.

  1. दमूनसो अपसो ये सुहस्ता वृष्णः पत्नीर्नद्यो विभ्वतष्टाः । सरस्वती बृहद्दिवोत राका दशस्यन्तीर्वरिवस्यन्तु शुभ्राः ॥ (ऋ. सं. ७-९६ [?]-२ [?]) damūnaso apaso ye suhastā vṛṣṇaḥ patnīr nadyo vibhvataṣṭāḥ | sarasvatī bṛhaddivota rākā daśasyantīr variyasyantu śubhrāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 7-96 [?]-2 [?]) Gloss: "(…) the wives of the bull, the rivers shaped by the Skilful One; may Sarasvatī, Bṛhaddivā and Rākā, the bright ones, giving, grant wide room." [tentative; the first half is hard for me to render with confidence]

  2. आ नो दिवो बृहतः पर्वतादा सरस्वती यजता गन्तु यज्ञम् । (ऋ. सं. ५-४३-११) ā no divo bṛhataḥ parvatād ā sarasvatī yajatā gantu yajñam | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-43-11) Gloss: "May worshipful Sarasvatī come to our sacrifice from heaven, from the great mountain."

  3. उभा नासत्या रुद्रो अध ग्नाः पूषा भगः सरस्वती जुषन्त । (ऋ. सं. ५-४६-२) ubhā nāsatyā rudro adha gnāḥ pūṣā bhagaḥ sarasvatī juṣanta | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-46-2) Gloss: "May both Nāsatyas, Rudra, the goddesses' wives, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Sarasvatī be pleased."

(The source's remark:) In these three Ṛks, too, Sarasvatī is the presiding deity of lightning. Griffith holds that in the first of these three Ṛks Sarasvatī is some one river — "Sindhu or Sarasvatī" — and that in the 2nd and 3rd [Ṛks of the group] the deity is clear. K. C. Caṭṭopādhyāya says that Ṛks 1–3 [of the group] apply to the Sindhu. These three Ṛks too, it is said, were composed by the descendants of the ṛṣi Atri. For the first Ṛk… (continues on the next page)

original p. 76

The deity-verses (concluded); where the river Sarasvatī flowed

…for the first Ṛk, Atri, or Atri's son Bhauma, is the ṛṣi; for the second Ṛk, Atri; for the third, Pratikṣatra, a descendant of Atri. In the second Ṛk Sarasvatī is addressed as having come from heaven ("divaḥ") and from the great mountain ("parvatāt") — [as the print has it]. In the first Ṛk, since the word "patnīḥ" ("wives") appears, the Bhāṣyakāra has regarded Sarasvatī and the other rivers as the wives of Indra.

  1. अग्निरिन्द्रो वरुणो मित्रो अर्यमा वायुः पूषा सरस्वती सजोषसः । (ऋ. सं. १०-६५-१) agnir indro varuṇo mitro aryamā vāyuḥ pūṣā sarasvatī sajoṣasaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-65-1) Gloss: "Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Vāyu, Pūṣan, Sarasvatī, in concert."

  2. विश्वे देवासः शृणवन्वचांसि मे सरस्वती सह धीभिः पुरंध्या । (ऋ. सं. १०-६५-१३) viśve devāsaḥ śṛṇavan vacāṃsi me sarasvatī saha dhībhiḥ puraṃdhyā | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-65-13) Gloss: "May the All-gods hear my words, and Sarasvatī with her thoughts and her plenty."

(The source's remark:) In these two Ṛks, too, Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech.

  1. यत्सारामं व्यपिबः शचीभिः सरस्वती त्वा मघवन्नभिष्णक् । (ऋ. सं. १०-१३१-५) yat sārāmaṃ vy apibaḥ śacībhiḥ sarasvatī tvā maghavann abhiṣṇak | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-131-5) Gloss: "When you drank the [sārāma-drink?] with your powers, O Maghavan, Sarasvatī tended you." [tentative; "sārāmam" is not rendered with confidence]

(The source's remark:) Since in this Ṛk Sarasvatī is spoken of as accompanying Indra, she may be understood either as the presiding deity of lightning or as the goddess of speech.

  1. गर्भं धेहि सिनीवालि गर्भं धेहि सरस्वति । (ऋ. सं. १०-१८४-२) garbhaṃ dhehi sinīvāli garbhaṃ dhehi sarasvati | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-184-2) Gloss: "Set the embryo, O Sinīvālī; set the embryo, O Sarasvatī."

(The source's remark:) Here it is only fitting to speak of Sarasvatī as the goddess of speech [as the print says — "vāg-devatā," though the verse is a prayer for conception].

Where the river Sarasvatī flowed. We shall now set out briefly, for those who wish to know, the discussion of where the river Sarasvatī flowed in that age. This account has been written following the publications: (1) R. D. Oldham in Journal of Asiatic Society Bengal, 1886, page 322; (2) C. F. Oldham, Journal of Royal Asiatic Society, 1893, page 51; (3) Maps of the Cambridge History of India, Vol. I, "Ancient India"; (4) Maps of Punjab published by the Surveyor-General of India; (5) "Ancient India as described by Megasthenes and Arrian." All as printed. In that age the river Sarasvatī was one large river. It arose in the Sirmur (the source's English: "Sismur") range in the Himālayas and flowed to the west and slightly south. At its source five small streams (small watercourses carrying water) joined and then flowed on as this river; for this reason it must have had the name "Pañcajātā." After flowing a little distance, a river called Dṛṣadvatī (the modern Chitrang) joined it, coming from the east. Āpayā is a tributary of the Dṛṣadvatī. The Sarasvatī of that time was to the south of the present Sarasvatī river (the source adds: rivers that flow in desert regions often change their beds). Into the present Sarasvatī river two small streams called Mārkaṇḍā (the source's English: "Markand") and Gaggar ("Ghaggar") … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." English words are as printed in the source. The Ṛg-vedic numbers in the list of senses of "vāja" below are in small Kannada numerals and they could not be read reliably; they are omitted rather than guessed, and the list should be completed from the page.

original p. 77

The course of the Sarasvatī (concluded); "vājebhiḥ"

Continuing from p. 76, "…two small streams, Mārkaṇḍā and Gaggar…" …these streams join her. Afterwards the Sarasvatī flowed on towards the south and west and finally joined the sea. The bed of the dried-up river now called Hakra (as printed) must have been the bed of the Sarasvatī of that time. It may have merged in the Sindhu by uniting with the river now called the Sutlej, or may have gone directly and joined the Sindhu. In that age the Sindhu lay far to the east of where it now is, and joined the sea near the gulf called the Rann of Kach (as printed). The scholar Max Müller, on the basis of the word "āsamudrāt" in Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-95-2 [?], holds that this Sarasvatī river went directly and joined the sea. Since the river flowed through sandy country before reaching the sea, it may well have been lost in the desert before reaching it (see Muir's Sanskrit Texts, Vol. II, p. 393, as printed). The account that the river was lost in the desert is given in the Mahābhārata (Vana-parva, in the description of the Tīrthayātrā) and also in the Manu-saṃhitā (2-21 [?]). For all these reasons it may be said that the present river Sarasuti is the Sarasvatī of old.

वाजेभिः (vājebhiḥ) — This word is used in this Ṛk in the sense "anna, āhāra" ("food"); there is the Taittirīya Śruti sentence "annaṃ vai vājaḥ" (अन्नं वै वाजः — "food indeed is 'vāja'"). Western scholars say that this word is used in many Ṛks in many different senses. Some of them are given here English as printed; the Ṛg-vedic references the source adds after each are not reproduced:

  1. Power, strength
  2. Swiftness (of the steeds)
  3. Combat
  4. Refreshment, food, nourishment
  5. Offering, food or drink of offering
  6. Horse
  7. One of the three Ṛbhus
  8. All the three Ṛbhus

Grassmann has given one long list for the various senses of this word, which occurs in many Ṛks; since it is very extensive, and since it is fitting to explain those senses in the respective places, there is no need to write it here. Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." English as printed; reference-numbers read with care but marked [?] where unsure.

original p. 78

"vājinīvatī," "yajñam," "vaṣṭu," "dhiyāvasuḥ"

वाजिनीवती (vājinīvatī) — The sense of this word follows that of the word "vājebhiḥ" given above. For it, Rāmanātha gives "Bestower of food"; Benfey, "filled up or rich with offerings"; Geldner, "rich with reward"; Rosen, "provided with food"; Ludwig, "rich with steed"; and the author of the Vedārtha-yatna, "Mounted on a charger" all as printed. Some say "vājinī" means the fruit-bearing land on a river bank that produces food, and "vājinīvatī" a river that gives people food and the like by supplying water to such fruitful land.

यज्ञम् (yajñam) — The word "yajña" is read among the fifteen words in the Nirukta (Ni. 3-1[?]) [as printed]. This word can be explained in two ways: (1) the worship of a deity by hymns of praise and the like; (2) a special rite performed by the subsidiary and sub-subsidiary rites, by the recitation of mantras, by offering up an animal, and by many homas. It is this second kind of rite that is generally described in the Vedas by the word "yajña."

वष्टु (vaṣṭu) — This word is the imperative (loṭ) third-person singular of the root "vaś kāntau" (to desire). The Bhāṣyakāra, giving the root the sense "apekṣā" ("expectation, wish"), states the main sense as "nirvahatv iti arthaḥ" — "let her bring (the sacrifice) to completion with all its parts." To support this he quotes the Aitareya Āraṇyaka sentence "yajñaṃ vaṣṭv iti yad āha yajñaṃ vahatv ity eva tad āha" (यज्ञं वष्ट्विति यदाह यज्ञं वहत्वित्येव तदाह — "when it says 'let her desire the sacrifice,' it says 'let her carry the sacrifice'," ऐ. आ. १-१-४). Geldner and Grassmann give "desire, wish for, make efforts, carry on to completion" ; the last sense is the right one here.

धियावसुः (dhiyāvasuḥ) — The Bhāṣyakāra explains this word thus: "dhiyāvasuḥ karma-prāpty-adhana-nimitta-bhūtā | vāg-devatāyās tathāvidhaṃ dhana-nimittatvam āraṇyaka-kāṇḍe śrutyā vyākhyātam | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasur iti vāg vai dhiyāvasuḥ" (धियावसुः कर्मप्राप्त्यधननिमित्तभूता । वाग्देवतायास्तथाविधं धननिमित्तत्वमारण्यककाण्डे श्रुत्या व्याख्यातं । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुरिति वाग्वै धियावसुः — ऐ. आ. १-१-४ — "Dhiyāvasuḥ: she who is the occasion of wealth to be gained by ritual action; that the goddess of speech is the occasion of wealth of this kind is explained by Śruti in the Āraṇyaka section: 'yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ' — speech indeed is dhiyāvasuḥ"). That is: "dhiyāvasu" means she who is the cause of the attaining of wealth, lordship and the like, obtained through sacrifices and other rites; the Bhāṣyakāra also quotes the Aitareya-Āraṇyaka sentence "yajñaṃ vaṣṭu" etc. to say that the goddess of speech is the cause of the attainment of wealth. And in considering the formation of the word he says: "dhiyā karmaṇā vasu yasyāḥ sakāśād bhavati sā dhiyāvasuḥ" (धिया कर्मणा वसु यस्याः सकाशाद्भवति सा धियावसुः) — the deity from whom the wealth that is to be obtained as the fruit of rites comes is called "dhiyāvasuḥ." Western scholars explain it with such words as : "Supporter of all by wisdom, recompenser of worship or religious ceremonies, bestower of riches, source of wealth, rich in sense or intellect, one rewarding for devotion excellent-minded." This word is used in the Ṛgveda only in eight Ṛks: Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-3-10; 1-3[?]-6 [?]; 10-[?]-3 [?]; and five further references, which are legibly numbered on the page in small Kannada numerals but which I have not been able to read with confidence and so do not give.
